questions.question: If orientation(a, b, c) > 0, where does point c lie relative to the directed line from a to b?
options: To the left of ray a->b (a counterclockwise turn)
To the right of ray a->b (a clockwise turn)
Exactly on the line through a and b
The sign alone can't tell you -- you also need the distance
questions.explanation: orientation(a,b,c) is the cross product of (b-a) and (c-a); a positive sign means a->b->c turns left (counterclockwise).

questions.question: A single fixed epsilon threshold safely distinguishes genuinely collinear points from nearly collinear points, regardless of coordinate magnitude.
questions.explanation: Rounding error in floating-point orientation tests scales with the magnitude of the coordinates, so no single epsilon is simultaneously tight enough for small inputs and loose enough for large ones.

questions.question: The technique that treats input coordinates as if infinitesimally perturbed by a fixed symbolic rule, so no predicate ever needs to return exactly zero, is called simulation of ____.
questions.explanation: Edelsbrunner & Mucke's 1990 'Simulation of Simplicity' gives a deterministic tie-breaking rule for degenerate predicate results, without changing the stored coordinates.

questions.question: Shewchuk's adaptive-precision predicates fall back to slower exact arithmetic:
options: On every single predicate evaluation, for safety
Only when the fast floating-point result's own error bound leaves the sign in doubt
Only when the input coordinates are negative
Never -- adaptive precision means floating point is always exact
questions.explanation: The fast double-precision path is taken whenever the computed magnitude exceeds its own error bound; the slow exact path only runs on the small fraction of near-degenerate inputs where the sign is genuinely uncertain.

questions.question: The ray-crossing point-in-polygon test classifies a query point as inside the polygon when the cast ray crosses the boundary:
options: It depends on the polygon's area
questions.explanation: An odd crossing count means the ray has passed from outside to inside an odd number of net times, so the query point is inside.

questions.question: Clamping the projection parameter t to [0, 1] when computing point-to-segment distance ensures the closest point stays on the segment rather than on the infinite line.
questions.explanation: Without clamping, a query point whose perpendicular foot falls outside the segment would report a distance to a point that isn't actually on the segment.

questions.question: Which condition guarantees the two circles do not intersect at all?
options: d is exactly equal to r1 + r2
d > r1 + r2, or d < |r1 - r2|
questions.scenario: Two circles have centers c1 and c2 with radii r1 and r2. The distance between centers is d.
questions.explanation: d > r1 + r2 means the circles are too far apart to touch; d < |r1 - r2| means one circle is entirely inside the other without touching -- both are the no-intersection cases from the triangle-inequality check.

questions.question: Graham scan sorts candidate points before building the hull by:
options: Polar angle around a pivot point
questions.explanation: Graham scan picks the lowest (or otherwise extreme) point as a pivot, sorts the rest by polar angle around it, then scans with a left-turn stack invariant.

questions.question: Graham scan's stack invariant requires every three consecutive points on the stack to always turn left (counterclockwise); if a right turn or straight line is found, the middle point is popped.
questions.explanation: That invariant is exactly what keeps the stack a valid convex chain at every step of the scan.

questions.question: Andrew's monotone chain sorts points primarily by ____ coordinate (breaking ties by the other coordinate) instead of polar angle.
questions.explanation: Sorting by x avoids computing any angles at all; the lower and upper hulls are then each built with the same left-turn stack rule Graham scan uses.

questions.question: In the closest-pair divide-and-conquer algorithm's merge step, each point in the y-sorted strip only needs to be compared against how many of the next points in that order to guarantee finding the true minimum distance?
questions.formula: A packing argument bounds the number of strip neighbors that can fit within the current best distance
questions.explanation: A packing argument shows at most 7 other points can fit within the current best distance in the strip's bounding region, bounding the strip check to O(n) overall.

questions.question: The closest-pair divide-and-conquer algorithm runs in O(n log n) overall, dominated by the initial coordinate sort plus the recursive merge/strip step.
questions.explanation: Each merge step's strip check is O(n) thanks to the packing bound, and there are O(log n) recursion levels, matching the initial sort's O(n log n).

questions.question: Rotating calipers finds the diameter of a convex polygon by walking:
options: A random sample of vertex pairs
questions.explanation: The polygon's diameter is always achieved by an antipodal pair, so the calipers only need to track those pairs as they rotate around the hull.

questions.question: The rotating calipers technique runs in O(n) time once the convex hull has already been computed.
questions.explanation: Each caliper direction only ever advances forward around the hull, so the whole rotation visits each vertex a bounded number of times.

questions.question: The sweep-line 'neighbor lemma' guarantees that the next unprocessed segment intersection must occur between segments that are:
options: The farthest apart in the sweep status order
Adjacent in the sweep status order
On the same side of the coordinate origin
Sorted by their right endpoint only
questions.explanation: If a third segment lay between two crossing segments in the status order, it would have had to leave that gap first -- an event that would already be queued -- so the crossing pair must be adjacent just before their event.

questions.question: A vertical segment has a single well-defined y-value in the sweep status at its own event x-coordinate, just like any other active segment.
questions.explanation: A vertical segment spans a y-interval at its own x, not a single point, so it needs a dedicated batching or range-query policy rather than the ordinary 'y at x' comparator.

questions.question: Bentley-Ottmann's classic complexity bound, reporting k intersections among n segments, is O((n + k) log ____).
questions.explanation: Each of the O(n + k) processed events costs O(log n) for its queue and status operations, giving the standard O((n+k) log n) output-sensitive bound.

questions.question: In a DCEL, following a half-edge's `twin` pointer moves you:
options: Along the same face's boundary to the next edge
Across the edge, to its other directed side
To the next vertex in angular order
To the previous face in the subdivision
questions.explanation: `twin` is the oppositely-directed half-edge representing the same geometric edge from the other side; `next`/`prev` are what move you along one face's boundary.

questions.question: For a connected planar embedding of a square with one diagonal (V=4, E=5, F=3, including the outer face), what does V - E + F equal?
questions.formula: Euler's formula for connected planar graphs: V - E + F
questions.explanation: Euler's formula for a connected planar embedding (including the outer face) always gives V - E + F = 2.

questions.question: In polygon overlay, the result A intersection B keeps exactly the faces that are:
questions.explanation: Each face's membership in A and in B is tracked independently after label propagation; intersection selects faces where both bits are true.

questions.question: Sutherland-Hodgman polygon clipping requires the clipping polygon to be convex.
questions.explanation: The algorithm represents the clip polygon as an intersection of inward half-planes, one per edge -- a representation that is only equivalent to the polygon's interior when it is convex.

questions.question: A simple polygon with n vertices always triangulates into exactly n - ____ triangles, no matter which valid diagonals are chosen.
questions.explanation: This count is invariant across all triangulations of the same simple polygon, provable by induction on any single diagonal split.

questions.question: The art-gallery theorem's floor(n/3) guard bound is proved by triangulating the polygon and then:
options: Randomly placing guards until every triangle is covered
3-coloring the triangulation's vertices and placing guards at the smallest color class
Running a greedy nearest-neighbor heuristic over the vertices
Solving a linear program over all triangle centroids
questions.explanation: Every triangle has one vertex of each color, so guards placed at the smallest color class (at most floor(n/3) vertices) see every triangle, and thus the whole polygon.

questions.question: The dual graph of a triangulated simple polygon (one node per triangle, an edge between triangles sharing a diagonal) is always a tree.
questions.explanation: Removing any diagonal separates that dual graph exactly as it separates the polygon into two pieces, which is the defining property of a tree.

questions.question: Helly's theorem in the plane says that if a finite family of convex sets has empty intersection, some ____ of them already have empty intersection.
questions.explanation: Planar Helly's theorem guarantees a small infeasibility certificate: at most three half-planes suffice to prove infeasibility in 2D.

questions.question: In Seidel's randomized incremental linear programming, backward analysis bounds the probability that processing the i-th constraint forces a basis repair by d/i, where d is the dimension.
questions.explanation: Among the first i randomly ordered constraints, only the at-most-d basis constraints could have been last, so the repair probability at step i is at most d/i -- the source of the algorithm's expected linear time for fixed d.

questions.question: Before adding fractional cascading, a 2D range tree answers an orthogonal range-reporting query in:
questions.explanation: O(log n) canonical nodes, each needing a further O(log n) binary search in its associated y-catalog, gives O(log^2 n + k) before cascading links the catalogs together.

questions.question: A balanced kd-tree's worst-case 2D range-reporting query time is O(sqrt(n) + k), while a 2D range tree's is O(log^2 n + k).
questions.explanation: This is exactly the tradeoff the two structures make: a kd-tree's compact O(n) space costs a worse worst-case query bound than the range tree's O(n log n)-space, polylogarithmic guarantee.

questions.question: A priority search tree answers ____-sided range queries by combining a binary-search-tree order on x with a min-heap order on y.
questions.explanation: The x-order gives two boundary paths for [a,b], and the heap order on y lets a subtree be pruned as soon as its minimum y exceeds the query's upper bound c.

questions.question: A centered interval tree stores each crossing interval at a node in two separate orderings: by left endpoint, and by:
questions.explanation: Sorting crossing intervals by left endpoint (for queries left of center) and by right endpoint (for queries right of center) lets a stabbing query stop scanning as soon as the ordering condition fails.

questions.question: A simplicial r-partition in the plane guarantees that any query line crosses only how many of the r partition simplices?
questions.explanation: The crossing-number bound is O(r^(1-1/d)); in the plane d=2, giving O(sqrt(r)) -- a line behaves like a 1D sheet crossing about r^(1/2) of the roughly grid-like cells.

questions.question: Partition trees and cuttings are the same idea applied in reverse: partition trees group points so a query hyperplane crosses few groups, while cuttings divide space so each cell conflicts with few input hyperplanes.
questions.explanation: One organizes points against future query hyperplanes; the other organizes space against a fixed set of input hyperplanes -- geometric duality makes the two views mirror each other.

questions.question: A uniform quadtree split to a fixed depth d always has how many leaves, regardless of the point distribution?
questions.explanation: A uniform quadtree splits every cell to depth d unconditionally, giving exactly 4^d leaves even if almost all of them are empty -- the reason adaptive variants exist.

questions.question: An adaptive quadtree's storage is O(m), where m is the number of materialized nodes, rather than the size of the imaginary finest uniform grid.
questions.explanation: Adaptive splitting only subdivides where local geometry demands it, so a dense region gets many small cells while an empty region stays as one large cell -- storage tracks actual detail, not grid resolution.

questions.question: In a trapezoidal-map history DAG, a Y-node tests:
options: Whether the query's x-coordinate is left or right of a stored endpoint
Whether the query point lies above or below a stored segment
The current depth of the search
questions.explanation: X-nodes branch on endpoint x-order; Y-nodes evaluate an orientation predicate against a stored segment to decide above/below -- together they route a query to its containing trapezoid.

questions.question: A randomized incremental trapezoidal map achieves expected O(n log n) construction time and expected space O(____).
questions.explanation: Backward analysis shows each insertion causes only O(1) expected structural change, so the total map and history size stays expected-linear in n.

questions.question: At a nondegenerate Voronoi vertex (general position), exactly how many sites are equidistant from it?
questions.explanation: Three sites lying on a common empty circle centered at the vertex is the generic case; four or more cocircular sites is the degenerate exception discussed explicitly in the article.

questions.question: Only sites on the convex hull of the input point set can have unbounded Voronoi cells.
questions.explanation: An extreme (hull) site 'wins' forever in some outward direction, while an interior site is always eventually beaten by some other site farther out -- unbounded cells and hull membership coincide.

questions.question: Flipping an illegal Delaunay edge replaces it with the diagonal that:
options: Makes both new triangles' circumcircles empty of the opposite vertices
questions.explanation: Legality is defined entirely by the empty-circumcircle test, not by length or slope; flipping restores that test locally, and repeated flips converge to a globally Delaunay triangulation.

questions.question: Among all triangulations of the same point set in general position, the Delaunay triangulation maximizes the minimum angle.
questions.explanation: This max-min-angle property is what makes Delaunay triangulations avoid unnecessarily thin triangles caused only by a poor diagonal choice, though it can't fix skinny geometry forced by the input itself.

questions.question: Under this series' point-line duality convention, if point p lies above line l, what is true of their duals p* (a line) and l* (a point)?
options: The dual point l* lies above the dual line p*
The dual line p* lies above the dual point l*
Duality does not preserve any vertical-order relationship
p* and l* must be parallel
questions.explanation: Duality preserves incidence but reverses vertical order: p above l if and only if l* is above p*.

questions.question: For n lines in general position, an arrangement has Theta(n^____) vertices, edges, and faces.
questions.explanation: V = C(n,2), E = n^2, and F = n(n+1)/2 + 1 are all Theta(n^2) -- a full arrangement can't be built faster than its own quadratic output size.

questions.question: Fractional cascading answers a predecessor query across k related sorted catalogs (each of size at most n) in:
questions.explanation: One binary search in the first augmented catalog, then constant-time bridge hops into every remaining catalog, replaces k independent O(log n) searches with O(log n + k) total.

questions.question: A Las Vegas algorithm may return an incorrect answer with small probability, while a Monte Carlo algorithm always returns a correct answer but has randomized running time.
questions.explanation: It's the reverse: Las Vegas algorithms are always correct with randomized time/space, while Monte Carlo algorithms have bounded cost but may be incorrect with small probability.

questions.question: For a triangulated, closed, connected 3D convex polytope with V vertices, E edges, and F faces, which relation holds?
questions.explanation: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 combined with double-counting edge-face incidences (3F = 2E for an all-triangular boundary) gives E = 3V - 6 and F = 2V - 4.

questions.question: In randomized incremental 3D hull construction, the horizon is exactly the boundary cycle of edges separating the connected patch of faces visible from the new point from the rest of the hull.
questions.explanation: The visible faces form a connected patch on the polytope, and its boundary -- the horizon -- is precisely where new triangles get stitched in to replace that patch.

questions.question: At one BSP node, the painter's algorithm decides draw order by:
options: Sorting all polygons globally by average depth once, before any traversal
Classifying the eye against the node's splitting plane and recursing far subtree, coplanar, then near subtree
Consulting a per-pixel z-buffer instead of the tree
Drawing every polygon in its original input order
questions.explanation: The eye's side of the splitting plane determines which child is 'far' and must be painted first -- this is why the same tree supports different back-to-front orders from different viewpoints.

questions.question: A binary space partition tree must always split space using axis-aligned planes, the same way a kd-tree does.
questions.explanation: A BSP splits with arbitrary hyperplanes, often chosen from an input polygon's own supporting plane -- axis-alignment is a kd-tree convention, not a BSP requirement.

questions.question: A workspace obstacle O, expanded for a translating robot with footprint R (reference point at the origin), becomes the configuration-space obstacle:
questions.explanation: Solving r + q = o for q gives q = o - r, i.e. the Minkowski sum of O with the REFLECTED robot -R -- the minus sign is not optional.

questions.question: For two convex polygons with m and n edges respectively, their Minkowski sum can be computed in O(m + n) time by merging their edge directions in angular order.
questions.explanation: This is exactly analogous to merging two sorted lists: normalize both polygons' starting vertices, then repeatedly append whichever edge vector has the smaller polar angle.

questions.question: A Euclidean shortest path among polygonal obstacles is called 'taut' because its interior bends occur:
options: At the midpoint of the nearest obstacle edge
At the centroid of whichever obstacle is closest
Nowhere -- an optimal path is always a single straight segment
questions.explanation: Anywhere a path bends in open free space, the bend can be shortened by a chord; only an obstacle vertex can pin a bend in place, which is exactly why the visibility graph captures every possible optimal bend.

questions.question: A* search over a visibility graph using straight-line distance to the goal as its heuristic is admissible and consistent, so it returns an optimal path.
questions.explanation: No obstacle-avoiding continuation can ever be shorter than the direct Euclidean distance, which makes the heuristic admissible, and the triangle inequality makes it consistent.

questions.question: In a well-engineered geometric predicate kernel, filtered predicates fall back to exact arithmetic:
options: On every call, for uniform safety
Only when the fast floating-point result's own error bound leaves the sign uncertain
Only when the user manually flags an input as degenerate
Never -- filtering replaces exact arithmetic entirely
questions.explanation: This is the same fast-path/slow-path discipline introduced with Shewchuk's predicates in Part 1's deep dive, now stated as a general engineering principle for any geometric kernel.

questions.question: A metamorphic test checks a known relationship between an input transformation and the resulting output change (e.g., translating the input should translate the result identically), rather than comparing against one fixed expected value.
questions.explanation: Metamorphic testing is especially valuable in geometry because many exact expected outputs are hard to hand-compute, but invariances like translation, scaling, and permutation are easy to state and check.

questions.question: Which structure best fits this workload?
options: A linear scan over all points for every query
A range tree, ideally with fractional cascading
Recomputing a convex hull for every query
questions.scenario: You have 2 million static 2D points and must repeatedly answer axis-aligned rectangular window queries at high volume, with strong worst-case latency requirements.
questions.explanation: Static data plus heavy, latency-sensitive query volume is exactly when paying O(n log n) space and preprocessing for a range tree (and its fractional-cascading speedup) pays off over a kd-tree's weaker worst-case query bound.

questions.question: Which structure directly targets this point-location workload?
options: A linear scan testing every parcel polygon
A randomized incremental trapezoidal map with its history DAG
A convex hull of all parcel vertices
questions.scenario: A GIS application must repeatedly answer 'which parcel contains this click?' against a large, rarely-changing parcel map.
questions.explanation: Trapezoidal maps are built exactly for static planar subdivisions with many repeated point-location queries, answering each in expected O(log n) via the history DAG.

questions.question: You need general polygon Boolean operations (union, intersection, difference) that must correctly support holes and multiple disconnected components. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Full sweep-line noding plus DCEL overlay and face labeling
questions.explanation: Sutherland-Hodgman only handles clipping against a convex window and can't represent multiple components or holes; general Boolean operations need the full overlay machinery from Part 8.

questions.question: Randomized incremental Delaunay construction is a Las Vegas algorithm: it always produces a correct triangulation, and only its running time varies with the random insertion order.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes it from a Monte Carlo algorithm -- the randomness here only affects expected performance, never correctness of the final triangulation.

questions.question: Your queries are triangular (not axis-aligned rectangular) range queries over a static point set. Which structure directly targets this?
options: A partition tree built from a simplicial r-partition
questions.explanation: Partition trees are designed exactly for simplex/halfspace queries, bounding how many partition simplices any query hyperplane can cross -- kd-trees and range trees are built around axis-aligned separability instead.

questions.question: This orientation function is buggy and can no longer distinguish left turns from right turns correctly. What's wrong with it?
options: It should subtract the second product term (a correct 2D cross product is ad - bc, not ad + bc)
It should use b[0] in the first term instead of a[0]
It should divide the result by 2 to get a true area
There is no bug -- this is a mathematically valid orientation test
questions.code:
def orientation(a, b, c):
    return (b[0] - a[0]) * (c[1] - a[1]) + (b[1] - a[1]) * (c[0] - a[0])
questions.explanation: The 2D cross product of (b-a) and (c-a) is (bx-ax)(cy-ay) - (by-ay)(cx-ax); replacing the minus with a plus computes a different (and geometrically meaningless) quantity, not a valid orientation sign.

questions.question: Once a visibility graph is built, Dijkstra's algorithm on it can still return a path that isn't actually collision-free if the underlying line-of-sight predicate incorrectly classified a blocked segment as visible.
questions.explanation: Graph search only optimizes over the edges it's given; it cannot detect or correct a geometry-layer bug that mistakenly added an edge that shouldn't exist -- this is why workspace replay/certification is a separate, independent check.

questions.question: For triangulating a simple polygon with no holes, which approach has a clean O(n log n) worst-case time guarantee?
options: Sweep-line monotone decomposition, then linear-time triangulation of each piece
Brute-force search over all possible diagonals
questions.explanation: Ear clipping is a simple O(n^2) baseline; sorting plus a sweep-line monotone decomposition (O(n log n)) followed by O(n) stack-based triangulation of each monotone piece gives the overall O(n log n) worst-case bound.

questions.question: The reference point used to define a robot's configuration space can be chosen arbitrarily, but it must then be used consistently across the Minkowski sum, the start/goal positions, and the final workspace replay.
questions.explanation: Changing the reference point translates every C-obstacle and every recorded configuration by the same amount, so consistency -- not any particular choice -- is what preserves correctness.

questions.question: Across this entire series -- predicates, sweep lines, DCELs, triangulations, and motion planning -- which single discipline recurs at every layer?
options: Always preferring floating point over exact arithmetic for speed
Defining a robust sign/predicate policy and a degeneracy convention before building any combinatorial structure on top of it
Avoiding all preprocessing in favor of brute-force queries
Using recursion instead of iteration wherever possible
questions.explanation: Every part in this series -- from Part 1's orientation predicate through Part 23's engineering discipline -- reduces to the same pattern: get the sign right and pick a degeneracy policy first, then build topology and algorithms that trust those decisions.
